books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals

primary_sources: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782)
Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776
Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790)

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which a distinct American identity developed in the period 1776–1800.

documents.title: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer
documents.source: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, 1782. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A French immigrant writing for European readers, describing what made Americans a new people.
documents.text: “What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. ... Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world.”

documents.title: Noah Webster, American Spelling Book
documents.source: Paraphrased from Noah Webster, American Spelling Book (1783). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A schoolbook for American children, showing how language was used to mark a separate culture.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Webster’s speller taught American schoolchildren simplified American spellings, such as theater for theatre, color for colour, honor for honour, and center for centre, because he held that American culture was separate from British culture.

documents.title: Abigail Adams to John Adams
documents.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A private letter from a wife to her husband in Congress, asking that new laws treat women fairly.
documents.text: “I desire you would remember the ladies and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the husbands. Remember, all men would be tyrants if they could.”

documents.title: George Washington, Farewell Address
documents.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, September 19, 1796. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A president leaving office, urging Americans to cherish their shared national name above local loyalties.
documents.text: “The name of American, which belongs to you in your national capacity, must always exalt the just pride of patriotism more than any appellation derived from local discriminations.”

documents.title: Pennsylvania Gradual Abolition Act
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Pennsylvania Gradual Abolition Act, March 1, 1780. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A state law, showing how far northern opposition to slavery went after the Revolution.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The act provided that children born to enslaved mothers on or after March 1, 1780, would become free once they reached the age of 28, while people already enslaved stayed enslaved for life.

documents.title: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes”
documents.source: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, 1790. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An essay by a woman writer, arguing that women’s minds were equal to men’s.
documents.text: “Are we deficient in reason? We can only reason from what we know, and if an opportunity of acquiring knowledge hath been denied us, the inferiority of our sex cannot fairly be deduced from thence.”

documents.title: Treaty of Greenville
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Treaty of Greenville, August 3, 1795. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A treaty imposed after an American military victory, showing the limits Native nations faced.
documents.text: Paraphrase: After General Wayne’s victory at Fallen Timbers in 1794, the confederation of Native nations signed the Treaty of Greenville, ceding most of what is now Ohio to the United States, though the Miami chief Little Turtle had argued for a smaller cession.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which a distinct American identity developed in the period 1776–1800, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the new republic seeking cultural independence after political independence, the spread of revolutionary ideas about equality, or the unfinished state of the nation in 1789.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about American identity.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents showing both the growth of a distinct identity and its limits.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as Charles Willson Peale’s museum in Philadelphia, Weems’s Life of Washington (1800), the Capitol in Washington, or the growth of slavery in the South.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Crèvecœur writing for Europeans, Adams writing privately to her husband, or Washington addressing the nation as he left office.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that a distinct identity grew in culture and letters while slavery, women’s legal status, and Native land loss kept it from reaching all Americans.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: A distinct American identity developed to a great extent between 1776 and 1800, because Americans built a shared culture, language, and founding story of their own, though that identity left out enslaved people, most women, and Native nations.
Context: Political independence in 1783 left Americans still reading British books, using British spellings, and looking to Europe for culture, so the new republic had to make a culture of its own.
A shared culture: Document 2 shows Webster teaching American spellings to schoolchildren, and Document 1 shows Crèvecœur describing Americans as a new people melted from many nations, so language and letters marked a separate identity.
A shared name: Document 4 shows Washington urging Americans to cherish “the name of American” above local loyalties, so the founding generation named the new identity itself.
Limits for women: Document 3 shows Abigail Adams asking for fairer laws for women, and Document 6 shows Murray arguing that women’s minds were equal, yet neither won women the vote or legal equality, so the new identity kept women in a domestic role.
Limits for enslaved people and Native nations: Document 5 shows Pennsylvania freeing only children born after 1780, and only at age 28, while Document 7 shows Native nations ceding most of Ohio after defeat, so the identity did not reach those it left out.
Outside evidence: Peale opened his Philadelphia museum in 1786 to show American portraits and natural wonders to the public, and the new Capitol in Washington, where Congress first met in 1800, gave the republic a home of its own.
Complexity: The identity was real and new, but it was a claim made mostly by and for white men, and its limits explain why later generations had to widen it.
